paragraphs.text: For roughly four hundred years, navigators trusted charts that showed islands nobody could ever find again. Historians now call these places phantom islands. They were rarely the product of deliberate deception. Most began as honest mistakes: a bank of low cloud mistaken for a coastline, a floating mass of pumice from an underwater volcano, or a simple error made when a hand-drawn chart was copied.

The best-documented case is Verlund, said to lie some 300 kilometres south-west of the Faroe Islands. It first appeared on a Venetian chart in 1482, drawn as a long green island with two harbours. Over the next century it was copied into at least nineteen atlases, and each copyist added details of his own: a river, a small town, even a population figure. By 1590, Verlund had acquired a name for its capital, although no account exists of anyone having landed there.

Why did such errors survive so long? The main reason is that map-makers worked largely from earlier maps rather than from fresh observation. Removing an island was risky, because a chart that left out real land could lead a ship onto rocks, whereas a chart that showed an imaginary island merely caused a captain to keep a careful lookout. For publishers, it was therefore safer to keep doubtful islands than to delete them.

Measuring position was another problem. Until the late eighteenth century, sailors could find their latitude fairly reliably by measuring the height of the sun at noon, but longitude was largely guesswork. A captain who sighted land might record its latitude accurately and still place it hundreds of kilometres too far east or west. When a second ship later reported land at the same latitude, cartographers often assumed both crews had seen different islands, and so one real island could appear twice on the same chart.

The process of removing a phantom island was slow and followed a recognised sequence. First, a ship would be sent to the reported position and fail to find land. Its captain would then file a report with the national hydrographic office, which would mark the island on its charts as 'existence doubtful'. Only after several independent searches had failed would the office finally delete the island altogether. Verlund was marked as doubtful in 1821 and removed in 1853, after a survey vessel spent eleven days sailing across the area.

Some phantom islands lasted well into the age of satellites. A small island in the Coral Sea was shown on several digital maps until 2012, when a research ship sailed straight through the spot where it was supposed to be and recorded water more than 1,400 metres deep. The error was eventually traced to a single typing mistake in a database built in the 1970s.

Modern cartographers point out that the story is not only one of failure. The effort to confirm or reject doubtful islands drove much of the systematic surveying of the world's oceans, and the records kept by hydrographic offices are now a valuable source for historians studying how scientific knowledge is checked and corrected.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the last twenty years, beekeeping has moved from the countryside onto the roofs of city buildings. Hotels, banks and universities in many European and North American cities now keep hives, and some city councils have begun to offer small grants to residents who want to start. Supporters say urban hives help to reverse the decline in bee numbers and reconnect city dwellers with nature. Not everyone is convinced.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The main argument for urban beekeeping is that cities can be surprisingly good places for bees. Parks, private gardens, street trees and balconies provide a wide variety of flowers that bloom at different times of year, while farmland is often planted with a single crop that flowers for only a few weeks. A 2019 survey in the city of Halden found that honey from rooftop hives contained pollen from more than 120 plant species, compared with about 40 in honey from nearby farms.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: However, ecologists warn that honeybees are only one of many pollinating insects, and not the ones most at risk. Wild bees, many of which live alone and nest in the ground, are declining much faster. Dr Ines Marlow, who studies wild pollinators, argues that adding large numbers of honeybee colonies to a city may harm wild species by competing with them for the same limited supply of flowers. In her view, planting more flowers would do more for pollinators than adding more hives.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Disease is another concern. Hives that are kept close together allow parasites and viruses to spread easily from one colony to the next, and from honeybees to wild bees that visit the same flowers. Professor Tomas Reyes, a bee pathologist, notes that many new urban beekeepers have little training and may not recognise the early signs of infection. He recommends that cities require beekeepers to register their hives so that outbreaks can be tracked.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Despite these doubts, most researchers agree that urban hives have value as a tool for education. School programmes that bring children onto a rooftop to watch a hive at work report strong interest in science and the environment. Lena Okafor, who runs one such programme, says that the hive is less important than the conversation it starts. The challenge for cities, she argues, is to keep that interest while making sure that the number of hives does not grow faster than the flowers available to feed them.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Most of us spend a surprising amount of our lives waiting: in queues at shops, on the phone to customer services, for buses and lifts. Researchers who study waiting have reached a conclusion that businesses are only beginning to act on: how long people wait matters less than how long they feel they have waited. In my view, this is the most useful idea the field has produced.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The principle was first demonstrated, according to a widely repeated account, at an office building where tenants complained that the lifts were too slow. Rather than install faster lifts, the managers placed mirrors beside the lift doors. The complaints stopped almost immediately, apparently because people had something to look at. Whether or not the story is true, it captures a finding that has since been confirmed in laboratory studies: occupied time feels shorter than unoccupied time.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Uncertainty also makes waiting feel longer. In a series of experiments, the psychologist Maria Delgado asked volunteers to wait in a room before a test. Those who were told how long the delay would last rated their wait as shorter and less annoying than those given no information, even when the second group actually waited for less time. Delgado concluded that an unexplained wait is more stressful than a longer wait whose length is known.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Fairness matters too. The sociologist Kwame Asante has studied how people react when someone arrives after them but is served first. He found that customers will accept a long wait in a single queue more readily than a shorter wait in several parallel queues, where they constantly compare their progress with others. Many supermarkets and banks have adopted the single 'snake' queue for this reason, although some customers still dislike it because the line looks longer.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Technology has added new complications. Apps that show the expected arrival time of a bus, for example, reduce uncertainty, and the economist Hannah Lindqvist found that bus users who had access to real-time information reported waits that felt about a fifth shorter. Yet Lindqvist also observed that when the predictions were wrong, satisfaction dropped below that of users with no information at all. I believe this shows that inaccurate information can be worse than none.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: None of this means that real waiting times are unimportant. A business that relies only on mirrors and progress bars, without actually reducing delays, will eventually lose customers. But the research suggests that the experience of waiting can be improved cheaply, and sometimes dramatically, by managing what people know and feel while they wait.
